prime.problem: A step that's right 95% of the time sounds reliable, but chain 20 of them and the task succeeds only about a third of the time. Faster steps don't help if the result is wrong and you have to redo the whole task.
prime.fits: Third agent card: the bottom of the agents overview's fraction. Tail latency and retries dealt with slow or failed calls; this card deals with calls that return a wrong answer, and why checking each step is the biggest lever.
prime.goal: Compute task success and time to a correct result for checked and unchecked designs, and pick where to add checks.

attend: Why does per-step success multiply rather than average across steps?
Why did τ-bench's pass^8 come out far above the 2% that independence predicts?
Why does a check with 2 retries raise one step from 90% to 99.9% for only 11% more calls?
Why does the careful slow model beat the fast one with an end check, but lose to the fast one with step checks?
When do retries not help at all?

must: Every unchecked step must go right → success = p<sup>N</sup> → falls fast with N (0.95<sup>20</sup> = 35.8%) → longer autonomous runs fail more
A check after each step catches a bad output immediately → only that step is retried → per-step success rises to 1 − (1 − p)<sup>3</sup> with 2 retries → 20 steps: 12.2% → 98.0%

Time to a correct result = attempt time ÷ success → a failed unchecked attempt repeats the whole task → checking each step (37.9 s) beats both a faster unchecked model (83.5 s) and a careful one (66.3 s)
elevated: Failures cluster on the same tasks → retries of a systematically wrong model fail the same way (τ-bench: ~25% pass^8 vs 2% if independent) → change something between tries or put a person at irreversible steps
reference: METR horizons (59 min at 50%, ~15 min at 80%, ~7-month doubling)

compress.prompt: From memory, write the three formulas: unchecked task success, checked step success with r retries, and time to a correct result. Use them to explain in three sentences why checking beats a better model.
checklist: checked with r retries: 1 − (1 − p)<sup>r+1</sup> per step
time to correct = attempt time ÷ success probability
checks confine a failure to one step instead of the whole task
retries assume independent tries; systematic errors need a change between tries

retrieve.q: Explain pass^k and why it's a better reliability measure for an agent than pass^1.
answer: pass^k: the chance all k tries of the same task succeed
pass^1 says how often it can succeed; pass^k says how consistently
an agent you rely on repeatedly needs consistency (61.2% pass^1 vs <25% pass^8)

retrieve.q: Walk through the arithmetic for the fast model with step checks: per-step time, per-step success, and the 37.9 s total.
answer: each step is retried until it passes: expected tries 1 ÷ 0.90

retrieve.q: Your coding agent's step checks cost 5 s each (a slow test suite), not 0.5 s. Is checking every step still worth it for the 10-step task? What would you change?
answer: checked: 10 × (2.91 + 5) ÷ 0.90 ≈ 87.9 s, now slower than the 83.5 s end check
run a fast subset of tests per step and the full suite at the end
or check only the risky steps

compare.q: Thinking raises p per call; checking catches failures after the fact. Which one changes the numerator and which the denominator of time to a correct result, and when would you use both?
answer: thinking makes each attempt slower (numerator up) but more likely right (denominator up)
checking adds a little time per step but turns failures into cheap retries
both: hard steps with cheap checks, e.g. a tricky bug fix with tests

compare.q: The repair loop validates JSON and retries with the error; this card validates each agent step and retries. What does feeding the error back add over a blind retry?
answer: a blind retry is a fresh draw with the same odds
feeding the error back changes the input, so the next try isn't identical
it attacks correlated failures, which blind retries can't

predict.q: Before computing: a 50-step task at p = 0.99 per step, unchecked. Is success above or below 60%? And with a check and one retry per step?
predict.answer: Unchecked: 0.99<sup>50</sup> ≈ 60.5%, just above 60%: even a 99% step loses 4 in 10 fifty-step tasks. With one retry per step: per-step 1 − 0.01<sup>2</sup> = 0.9999, and 0.9999<sup>50</sup> ≈ 99.5%.

apply.task: Pick an agent task you run (a refactor, a data pipeline, a support flow). List its steps, estimate p for each, and mark which ones you can check cheaply (tests, types, schema, a dry run). Compute unchecked success (product of p's) and checked success with 2 retries on the checkable steps.
apply.done: You have a step table with p and a check (or none), two task-success numbers, and the one step where adding a check raises success most.
apply.hint: Steps without a check still multiply in unchecked; the weakest unchecked step usually dominates.

reflect: Which prediction did you get wrong: how a 99% step fares over 50 steps?
What couldn't you explain cleanly: why τ-bench's pass^8 beat the independence prediction?
Which relationship is still fuzzy: checks → per-step success, or per-step success → time to a correct result?
Which step in your own agent work has no check, and why?
What cheaper model could handle your easy steps if a check catches its misses?
